name: hillfort

attributes.attribute: Celtic archaeological site of high, usually circular earthen walls on hills, also called rath, dun, liss, or cashel
built from roughly 700 BCE through the early Middle Ages and tied to settlement, trade, government, and ceremony
more than 30,000 remain, each housing from several dozen to several score residents
somewhat larger than other hillforts and usually built on high, easily defensible ground

sources: Aalen, F. H. A. Man and the Landscape in Ireland. London: Academic Press, 1978.

text: Hillforts are Celtic archaeological sites. People also call them raths, ráths, duns, dúns, lisses, and cashels. Hillforts stand throughout Ireland and, to some extent, Britain. Builders raised high earthen walls. The walls were usually circular and stood mainly on hills. Archaeological findings suggest that wooden buildings may have stood on these walls. Builders made hillforts from roughly 700 BCE through the early Middle Ages. The sites connected to Celtic settlement, trade, government, and ceremony. More than 30,000 hillforts remain standing. Each would have housed from several dozen to several score residents. Many Irish towns still carry the name of the local hillfort. Examples include Rathangan, Lisdoonvarna, Lisadell, and Dunmore. Cashels are somewhat larger than other hillforts. They usually stand on high, easily defensible ground. The earthen walls simplified the defense of the site. Some hillforts are important in myth. Examples include Grianan Aileach, Emain Macha, Tara, and Cruachan.
